fields.title: Temp: shorter onboarding, lower retention
fields.summary: Registrations went up, but weekly retention dropped. Decide what to recommend tomorrow.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you recommend to the team, and what will you walk away from?
fields.brief/role: You are a growth product manager at Temp.
fields.brief/company: Temp is a fictional habit tracking app: 900 thousand monthly active users, team of 40 people.
fields.brief/context: Ten days ago, a new onboarding flow was rolled out to everyone: it went from nine screens to four—goal setting and creating the first habit were moved into the app itself. Registration completion rose from 61% to 78%, and everyone celebrated. Yesterday, an analyst reported that weekly retention for the new cohort is noticeably lower. The head of product expects a recommendation at tomorrow's meeting.
fields.brief/objective: Do not lose first-week retention and, if possible, keep the registration gains.
fields.brief/constraints: Two developers for the sprint. Ten days of data, two full weekly cohorts, and one of them is not closed yet.
fields.brief/task: Decide what to do next, and name what you are sacrificing.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Improved one step? Look at the entire user journey
fields.learnTakeaway/body: An increase in registration completion means nothing on its own: you need to measure the yield against incoming traffic. When two metrics diverge, the answer is almost always in a breakdown—here, it is the share of users who created their first habit. And the noisier the data, the cheaper your first action should be: a one-day card verified over two weeks is better than a three-day rework based on the same grounds.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Old flow (four weeks before release): registration completion 61%, Day 7 retention 34%, Day 30 — 19%.

New flow (ten days): completion 78%, Day 7 retention 27%.

Active users per 1,000 visits: was 207, now 211—a difference within the noise margin, which the analyst estimated at ±14.

Breakdown for the new flow: created a habit during the first session — retention 41%, did not — 12%. In the old flow, 88% had a habit by the end of registration; in the new flow, 46% by the end of Day 1.

Analyst's note: "Ten days is just a little over one cohort. Plus, on Day 3 we were featured in the app store collection, bringing in about 30 thousand installs."
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
A researcher conducted five 20-minute calls with users who went through the new flow.

Three out of five said that after registration, the app looks "empty." Two of those three could not explain what it was for.

Two had created a habit by the time of the call: both found the plus button on their own in the first minute, and both clearly described why they needed the app.

One user, after watching a recording of the old flow, said it was "endless" and preferred the new one—even though he still hadn't created a habit.

Four out of five installed the app on the days when it was featured in the store collection.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
The new flow is behind a feature flag: rolling everyone back to nine screens takes minutes, not a day.

A partial rollback is not that simple: goal setting and habit creation were removed in a single change, and the state machine was rewritten around it. Splitting them back apart is about three days plus testing.

A card on the main screen that nudges a newcomer to create their first habit takes about one day of work.

There was no dedicated event for "habit created in the first session" before the release: today's breakdown was compiled retroactively by creation time.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Temp sells subscriptions on Day 14. Of those who reach Day 14, about 6% pay, and payment is strongly correlated with having at least one active habit.

In three weeks, paid acquisition starts, which will roughly double the flow of new users for a month; the budget is already approved.

The Head of Growth wrote that she doesn't want to "pour budget into a leaky bucket."

Revenue isn't showing anything yet: the first new cohort will only reach Day 14 in four days.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Keep the new flow and prompt the first habit
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Ship a card on the main screen that leads newcomers to create a habit, and see if the habit creation rate and retention recover.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The card ships in two days. Over two weeks, the share of newcomers with a habit by the end of Day 1 grows from 46% to 71%.
Day 7 retention in this cohort is 33%, almost matching the old flow, while registration completion stays high at 76%. Both metrics are preserved.
The analyst honestly warns that the card's effect cannot yet be isolated from the fading wave from the app store feature, and you agree to launch paid acquisition with a proper control group.
Trade-off: you acted on a hypothesis rather than a proven cause, and you will only get a definitive answer with the next cohort.
fields.decisionOptions/1/label: Bring habit creation back into onboarding
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Spend three engineering days to split the change and keep a short registration without goal setting, but with habit creation included inside.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Four days later, a six-screen flow goes live: without goals, but with habit creation.
Registration completion sits at 71%—lower than 78%, but higher than the original 61%. Day 7 retention is 33%.
The decision is fundamentally right, but costlier than necessary: a one-day card achieved the same effect. The difference is that here you paid with three days of dev time and a slice of registration gains.
Everything is ready before paid acquisition starts, which is the main win.
Trade-off: almost an entire sprint was spent on something that could have been tested for less.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Change nothing and investigate for two weeks
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Leave the flow as is, wait for a second full cohort, conduct more interviews, and come back with clean data.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Two weeks later, the data is indeed cleaner: retention in the new cohort is 28%, confirming the habit breakdown.
However, paid acquisition has already started by then, and a doubled flow of new users went through the same onboarding—roughly 60 thousand people with 27% retention instead of 33%.
The Head of Growth reminds you of her email, making for a difficult conversation.
Trade-off: caution was justified, but its cost was an entire cohort purchased with the approved budget.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Roll back to the old flow
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Toggle the feature flag back to nine screens, restore known retention, and return to the redesign later with a proper experiment.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The rollback takes minutes, retention returns to 34%, and registration completion drops back to 61%.
Active users per 1,000 visits remain unchanged—207 versus 211: by this metric, you ended up right where you started.
Meanwhile, the breakdown had already shown that the problem wasn't the number of screens, but the absence of a first habit, and you set that insight aside.
Trade-off: safe and reversible, but the entire change was rolled back instead of just the part that was hurting retention.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Feedback was not broken down by what the person was trying to do
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: The volume of a complaint was mistaken for problem severity
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: An average was mistaken for a description of user behavior
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: A metric was named without an objective or observable signal
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: Interview questions ask about the future or about "usually"
fields.rubric/remediation/5/gap: Research was planned without a hypothesis it could disprove
fields.rubric/remediation/6/gap: A customer request was mistaken for their underlying problem
